1.pericope_label: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying, Stand in the gate of the Lord’s house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the Lord, all ye of Judah, that enter in at these gates to worship the Lord. Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place

schools.summary: Sets the sermon in its political and literary place, one voice dividing the whole discourse into three sections and giving its argument in advance, the other refusing to fix a date absolutely while reading the prevalence of idolatry and a possible reference to the invader as fitting the later reign; both work the language of the demand closely, making the verb mean to make one's way good and separating general habits from separate acts.

Reads the occasion from the practice of the feasts, since on ordinary days only the city's inhabitants frequented the courts, and makes the whole object of the sermon the exposure of an expiation that sent every man home as though he had God propitious to him; disputes the promise in the translating, preferring I will dwell with you in this place on the authority of the older versions, and grounds the demand in the title of hosts.

Fixes the date in the first year of Jehoiakim, who restored idolatry and maintained bad priests and worse prophets, holds the section to run three chapters on, and identifies the gate as the east one, the public place of going out and coming in where the people were wont to assemble.

Supposes the occasion one of the three feasts, weighs the cost of preaching such a message inside the priests' precincts, and requires an amendment universal, constant and sincere rather than partial or hypocritical, since the tree must be made good to make the fruit good.

debates.question: When, and under which king, was the sermon delivered?

positions.view: in the first year of Jehoiakim, who, far from following his pious father, restored idolatry and maintained bad priests and worse prophets

nothing in the discourse absolutely fixes a date, but the prevalence of idolatry and possibly a reference to the invader already at hand fit Jehoiakim's reign rather than Josiah's, and a later chapter's report of a Shiloh prophecy from the beginning of that reign suggests this discourse drew down the king's displeasure
leaves the date alone and sets out the three-section structure of the whole discourse instead

debates.question: In which gate did the prophet stand?

positions.view: the eastern gate, the principal of them all, on the authority of a Jewish commentator
the east gate, the public place of going out and coming in, where the people were then wont to assemble
the inner gate of one of the courts, possibly the one by which the king entered in ceremonial state, a priest having access to every part of the building
one of the three gates of the inner court, perhaps the one where Baruch afterwards read the prophecies aloud

debates.question: What is promised to those who amend their ways?

positions.view: only the continuance of blessings already enjoyed; the English suggests something new, and the words should be rendered I will let you dwell
the verb should be read the other way, I will dwell with you in this place, following the older versions, since their whole boast was that God dwelt among them because the house was his
the plain sense, that only good endeavours give a sure title to a long lease of the land

outliers.reading: Alone weighs what the place of delivery cost the man who spoke there, since such a message inside the priests' precincts would affront them and expose the prophet to their rage, and he cannot be faithful if he fears the face of man; and requires an amendment universal, constant and sincere rather than partial or hypocritical, the tree being made good in order to make the fruit good.

Makes the sermon's whole object the exposure of a false expiation: after the feast every man went home as though, having made his expiation, he had God propitious to him, and the answer is that God does not regard the external rites at all; he hears in the promise an implied contrast, that the people would not long survive unless they sought another way to pacify God.

themes: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying,
Stand in the gate of the Lord’s house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the Lord, all ye of Judah, that enter in at these gates to worship the Lord.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place.

4.pericope_label: Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the Lord, The temple of the Lord, The temple of the Lord, are these. For if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye throughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour; if ye oppress not the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, then will I cause you to dwell in this place. Behold, ye trust in lying words, that cannot profit

schools.summary: Hears in the threefold naming of the temple the burden of the false prophets' discourses and possibly the iteration of a litany, a people harping on the building's greatness and predicting its perpetuity while giving no thought to the presence it symbolised; narrows the justice demanded to helping one man to his rights against another, groups the stranger, fatherless and widow as the great representatives of the helpless, and notes that the Hebrew accentuation attaches the words of perpetuity to the gift made to the fathers rather than to the promise of dwelling.

Takes the plural of the three parts of the building and turns the repetition into a triple rampart, a city walled three times being thought impregnable; has the prophet address the judges first, requiring judgment without favour or hatred and unmoved by bribes, makes the treatment of the helpless the test of a government, and reads the words of falsehood as an impious divorce of the sign from the reality it was instituted to carry.

Reports the Chaldee paraphrase that turns the clause into a liturgy while preferring to read it as the people's own conviction of safety, takes the plural of the courts and the house and the holiest as pointed at from the gate, renders the condition literally as making good one's ways so that no half-hearted work is admitted, and counts three sins in the demand for justice.

debates.question: Why is the temple named three times over?

positions.view: the Chaldee turns the clause into a liturgy ending in thrice in the year ye shall appear, which the Targumist supposed the reason; but the words rather express the people's conviction that they were safe while the temple service continued
it was the burden of the false prophets' discourses, and possibly the solemn iteration of the words in the supplicants' litanies
the three parts of the building, court, holy place and innermost, make a triple defence, a city walled not once but three times being thought impregnable
the courts and the house and the holiest, which the prophet in the gate points at as with his finger

debates.question: What does the condition of amendment actually require?

positions.view: literally, if in making good ye fully make good your ways: God will no longer admit half-hearted work and will not accept a partial reformation
the duties of the moral law, more acceptable to God than legal sacrifices when done from love, in faith, and to his glory
the justice meant is helping one man to his rights against another, the law having attached penalties to the oppression of those who most needed protection
the judges are addressed first, and must judge without favour or hatred and unmoved by bribes

debates.question: What are the words about perpetuity attached to?

positions.view: the English punctuation attaches them to the promise of dwelling, but the Hebrew accentuation to the gift made to the fathers, intended to last but forfeited by the people's guilt
to the verb, so that they remain from age to age as their fathers did

outliers.reading: Reads the lying words as an impious divorce rather than a mere boast: the sacrifices were instituted to show men they deserved death and to send them for mercy, so that to lay hold on the naked sign while overlooking the reality turns the institution to a contrary end; and records that several of the older versions give the temple phrase twice rather than thrice and put the verb in the singular.

Glosses the phrase about a man and his neighbour as the Jewish idiom for one man and another, and groups the stranger, the fatherless and the widow as the great representatives of the poor and helpless, most in need of man's justice and of divine protection.

themes: Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the Lord, The temple of the Lord, The temple of the Lord, are these.
For if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye throughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour;
If ye oppress not the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, and shed not innocent blood in this place, neither walk after other gods to your hurt:
Then will I cause you to dwell in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers, for ever and ever.
Behold, ye trust in lying words, that cannot profit.

9.pericope_label: Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and burn incense unto Baal, and come and stand before me in this house, and say, We are delivered to do all these abominations? Is this house become a den of robbers in your eyes? But go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel. And I will cast you out of my sight

schools.summary: Works the string of infinitives as grammar before it is doctrine, one voice complaining that the English obscures the idiom and the other reading the query before the verbs as wonder and indignation while counting the commandments breached, three of the second table and two of the first; supplies the geography of the den of robbers, admits that no historical notice of Shiloh's fall survives, and reads the command to go and look as rhetoric that strengthens the threat.

Turns the grammar into an accusation, since men who take sacrifices out of their plunder to expiate their crimes make God a participator in the robbery, and gives the den its logic, that robbers dare not use the sword in the open for fear of the laws and take their liberty only where they are hidden; disputes which ruin of Shiloh is meant, preferring the desolation that followed the removal of the ark because only the earlier makes the argument complete, and observes that the going is a taking of the place into the mind rather than a journey.

Keeps to the history and the plain sense: the sanctuary at Shiloh was let fall to the Philistines and set up in the house of their idols for the iniquity of the priests and the people, and those who had appeared with their sacrifices thought themselves privileged to return to their wickedness.

debates.question: What is the force of the string of verbs in the catalogue of crimes?

positions.view: the English obscures the emphasis of the idiom, which gives them as infinitives: What, to steal, to murder, to burn incense to Baal, and then have ye come before me
the query before them expresses wonder and indignation, and the breaches run through three commandments of the second table and then two of the first
the grammar is an accusation, since men who take sacrifices out of their plunder to expiate their crimes make God a participator in the robbery
the list divides at the same point, the first sins against the second table and what follows against the first

debates.question: What did the worshippers mean by saying they were delivered?

positions.view: a different pointing yields Deliver us, reproducing the people's own prayer with indignant scorn; keeping the word, they left the fast feeling saved, and the prophet repeats it ironically, delivered not from their abominations but as if set free to do them
they never said it in words at all; a version renders it a petition, but the declarative sense is to be preferred
having appeared with their sacrifices they thought themselves privileged to return to their wickedness

debates.question: What does the precedent of Shiloh prove, and which ruin is meant?

positions.view: the desolation that followed the removal of the ark rather than the later devastation of the northern captivity, since only the earlier makes the argument complete; and the place is older, excelling in antiquity rather than merely equalling
no historical notice of the event survives, and the command to go and look is rhetoric strengthening the threat, since sacredness does not save a place from overthrow
the sanctuary was let fall to the Philistines and set up in the house of their idols, for the iniquity of the priests and the people
the place had never been a centre of light and purity, and this reference more than anything else in the sermon provoked the wrath of priest and people
the going is not local but a taking of the place into the mind

outliers.reading: Gives the den of robbers its setting, a country whose limestone caves had always sheltered outlaws, and makes those who thronged the courts, priests and prophets among them, such robbers soothing their consciences by their worship; and observes that the phrase about rising early belongs to this prophet alone and in its bold anthropomorphism takes the highest form of human activity, waking from sleep and beginning at dawn, to picture the like in God.

Supplies the logic of the comparison rather than its colour: robbers dare not use the sword in the open because they fear the laws, and take their liberty only where they are hidden, so that had there been no temple some integrity might have survived on common feeling alone; and reads the rising early as a father's care, God claiming as his own the labour done through his prophets.

themes: Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and burn incense unto Baal, and walk after other gods whom ye know not;
And come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, We are delivered to do all these abominations?
Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, even I have seen it, saith the Lord.
But go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel.
And now, because ye have done all these works, saith the Lord, and I spake unto you, rising up early and speaking, but ye heard not; and I called you, but ye answered not;
Therefore will I do unto this house, which is called by my name, wherein ye trust, and unto the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I have done to Shiloh.
And I will cast you out of my sight, as I have cast out all your brethren, even the whole seed of Ephraim.

16.pericope_label: Therefore pray not thou for this people, neither lift up cry nor prayer for them: for I will not hear thee. Seest thou not what they do in the cities of Judah? The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead their dough, to make cakes to the queen of heaven. Behold, mine anger and my fury shall be poured out upon this place, and shall not be quenched

schools.summary: Reads the prohibition as the checking of an intercession already rising in the prophet's heart, identifies the goddess precisely as a kind of Assyrian Artemis joined to the moon and distinct from Ashtoreth, and settles the question of provocation partly by grammar, taking the pronoun reflexively, and partly by objecting to the translators, whose supplied words complete the sense but mar the abrupt force of the original.

Makes the ban a mercy to the prophet, who had not divested himself of human feelings and might have been tardier in denouncing vengeance had pity been left to melt him, refuses to settle the identity of the goddess since a missing letter would give the workmanship of the heavens rather than a queen, and denies that God can be provoked as men are, whether from the absence of perturbation in him or from the fact that he could be without their worship and suffer no loss.

Takes the moon plainly, setting the sun as king against the moon as queen, lays out the household's division of labour in the idolatrous service and turns it into a reproach on Christian families, and reads the unquenchable fire as showing that the resolution is not to be revoked.

Reads the prohibition as evidence of the weight prayer carries, since God bespeaks his prophet beforehand rather than let such prayers lie unanswered, and draws from the idolaters' diligence the lesson that we should be as careful to teach our children the truths of God as many are to teach the mysteries of iniquity.

debates.question: Why is the prophet forbidden to pray, and did he obey?

positions.view: an intercession like the one Moses offered was already rising in his heart and had to be checked, since judgment must have its way and the discipline do its work

the prohibition shows the weight such prayers carry, God bespeaking his prophet beforehand because he would not have them lie unanswered; it is an ill omen when the spirits of ministers are restrained from praying for a people
it is a mercy to the prophet himself, who had not divested himself of human feelings and might have been tardier in denouncing vengeance had pity been left to melt him
how terrible must a place be where God refuses the spirit of supplication on its behalf
the prophet certainly did still pray, for a remnant, though not for the revoking of the decree

debates.question: Who is the queen of heaven?

positions.view: a kind of Assyrian Artemis, joined to the moon and to the symbolic worship of the reproductive powers of nature, whose ritual probably resembled the Babylonian one in its impurities, and to be distinguished from Ashtoreth, whose name signifies a star and belongs to another planet
most probably the moon, though perhaps not to the exclusion of the sun and the planets
the moon, the sun being looked on as king and she as queen
undecidable: a missing letter would give the workmanship of the heavens rather than a queen, and every man may enjoy his own opinion, though the moon is likelier if the title stands

debates.question: In what sense can God be provoked?

positions.view: in no sense proper to men, since there is no such perturbation in God, and though he does what men do in anger the damage of sin falls on the sinner
the pronoun is reflexive: instead of vexing him they vex themselves, the consequences of their idolatry falling on their own head
he could be without their worship and suffer no loss, so their fury returns upon them
the translators' supplied words complete the sense but mar the abrupt force of the original: is it not themselves, to the confusion of their own faces?

outliers.reading: Traces the verb for pouring out, used elsewhere of a plague of rain and here of a great shower of fire, and notes that it had been on Josiah's lips when he heard the judgments denounced in the newly found book of the law.

Asks why the sentence should reach innocent beasts and trees and fruit, and answers that the world was made for man, so the symptoms of wrath are extended through all the elements to show how displeased God is with him.

themes: Therefore pray not thou for this people, neither lift up cry nor prayer for them, neither make intercession to me: for I will not hear thee.
Seest thou not what they do in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?

The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead their dough, to make cakes to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto other gods, that they may provoke me to anger.
Do they provoke me to anger? saith the Lord: do they not provoke themselves to the confusion of their own faces?

Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, mine anger and my fury shall be poured out upon this place, upon man, and upon beast, and upon the trees of the field, and upon the fruit of the ground; and it shall burn, and shall not be quenched.

21.pericope_label: Put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices, and eat flesh. For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices: but this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice. But they hearkened not, but walked in the counsels and in the imagination of their evil heart, and went backward, and not forward

schools.summary: Keeps the sarcasm short, add one kind to another and partake of the feast, all fruitless without repentance and holiness, and does the heaviest work on the denial that sacrifice was ever commanded, pressing the preposition, which is literally with a view to, and arguing that the ritual came after a spiritual and ethical law partly as a concession and partly as an education; adds that they neglected what was foremost and cardinal in it, with a textual note on two words that stand in apposition.

Hears God excluding himself from the feast, ye sacrifice to yourselves and not to me, and grants the objection to the denial its full force, since the sacrifices promoted penitence and were pledges of expiation, before answering that the prophet speaks to the ideas of men who had vitiated them, God having joined the sign to its end where man may not separate; supplies the aggravation that a people bound by creation and providence were bound further by distinguishing blessings.

Makes the command a plain refusal, so that the beasts set apart may as well be slain for common nourishment and what was peculiar to God be done with as they please, holds the denial of sacrifice comparative only, and counts the descent in four steps from not hearkening to a decline that left them more profligate than their fathers.

Turns the whole burnt offering into a peace offering they may dine on, since a meal's meat or two is all the good they are likely to get by it, and reaches the denial from the order of the books, the moral precepts standing before the ceremonial and the sacrificial law opening as though it meant rather to regulate sacrifice than to require it.

debates.question: How is the command to pile the offerings up and eat to be taken?

positions.view: turn the whole burnt offering into a peace offering you may dine on, since a good meal's meat or two is all the good you will get by it; or else, keep your sacrifices to yourselves and let them be served at your own table
a plain refusal of both sacrifice and oblation, so the beasts set apart may as well be slain for common nourishment
add one kind to another and partake of the feast, all of it fruitless without repentance and holiness
God excludes himself: ye sacrifice to yourselves and not to me; and the verb may come from a root meaning to sweep together, which suits the contempt better
ironical throughout: they may do what they will even with what was peculiar to God, who will have none of it

debates.question: How can God say he commanded nothing about sacrifice at the coming out of Egypt?

positions.view: the preposition is literally with a view to, and sacrifice was never the end contemplated: the first promulgation set out a spiritual and ethical religion, and the ritual came afterwards, partly as a concession to the temper shown in the worship of the calf and partly as an education
the order of the books settles it, the moral precepts standing before the ceremonial, and the sacrificial law opening as though it meant rather to regulate sacrifice than to require it
the denial is comparative, the offerings condemned not in themselves but against obedience
the prophet speaks to the ideas of men who had vitiated them: God joined the sign to its end, and it is not in man's power to separate what he has connected

debates.question: What does going backward rather than forward describe?

positions.view: a descent in four steps, from not hearkening, to not inclining the ear, to walking after an evil heart's motions, to a decline that left them more profligate than their fathers
the resolve rather than the drift, since they not only followed their own ways but made resolutions to walk in them, leaving no excuse but the wish to be wiser than God
the whole sacrificial system, even at its best and apart from its corruptions, a retrograde movement away from the first and purely spiritual covenant
a neglect of what was foremost and cardinal in the law

outliers.reading: Measures the influence of this teaching on later Jewish thought from the synagogue lectionary, where this passage stands as the lesson from the prophets appointed to follow the sacrificial portion of the law; that service, being in the nature of the case the work of scribes and prophets rather than priests, bore witness to the spiritual truth symbolised in sacrifice and not to the perpetuation of the symbol.

Notes that the two words for their walking stand in apposition rather than in subordination, that the Greek could not admit this and dropped the second, and that several critics have followed it in deleting the word as a gloss.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices, and eat flesh.
For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices:
But this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people: and walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you, that it may be well unto you.
But they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear, but walked in the counsels and in the imagination of their evil heart, and went backward, and not forward.

25.pericope_label: Since the day that your fathers came forth out of the land of Egypt unto this day I have even sent unto you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they hearkened not unto me, but hardened their neck: they did worse than their fathers. Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee. This is a nation that obeyeth not the voice of the Lord their God

schools.summary: Presses the history of prophecy itself, arguing from the free bestowal of the gift as early as the wilderness and the honour paid to seers before Samuel that what was new in his ministry was the name and the organisation rather than the gift; finds the survey too rapid to fix which generations are compared and settles for a progressive deterioration, renders both clauses of the commission concessively, and gets the same sense from the consecutive form.

Reads the daily rising as God's persistence across generations and refuses the plea that descent from corrupt fathers extenuates, since continued indulgence in vice does not serve for a precedent and the dead are joined to the living to make the guilt twofold; finds the indignation in the change of person, and marks the change of manner by which the prophet is bidden not to address them but to pronounce sentence, the word for nation being the one Scripture sets against the chosen people.

States the principle that the church has never wanted teachers raised up and sent by God, sums the failure as a loss of both means, since blessings and corrections have been equally thrown away, and puts the verdict shortest, that there is no believing them in anything they say.

debates.question: Was there a continual succession of prophets from the exodus onward?

positions.view: yes, and the apparent difficulty of Samuel's prominence as the first to bear the name is met by the free bestowal of the gift as early as the wilderness and the honour paid to seers before him: the name and the organisation, not the gift, were new in his ministry
the church of God has never wanted teachers raised up and sent by him
the daily rising is God's own persistence across generations, the children succeeding their fathers in the same corruptions until the imitation became perpetual
the disobedience runs unbroken from the first coming out of Egypt

debates.question: Whose generation is said to have done worse than whose?

positions.view: the survey is too rapid to say whether the comparison lies between the generation that came out and their immediate followers or between those and their successors; probably the whole history was one of progressive deterioration climaxing in the prophet's own time

the degree matters less than the plea it supports: descent from corrupt fathers is urged as an extenuation by those who plead antiquity, but continued indulgence in vice does not serve for a precedent, and the dead are joined to the living to make the guilt twofold

debates.question: How is the commission to speak to those who will not hear to be rendered?

positions.view: both clauses concessively: though thou shalt speak, yet they will not hearken; though thou shalt call, yet they will not answer
the consecutive form reads literally speak to them and they will not hearken, meaning even if thou speakest
the indignation lies in the change of person, God having said your fathers and I sent unto you and now saying they hearkened not, as one wearied with addressing a stupid people

outliers.reading: Weighs what the commission cost the man who carried it, since the prophets did not divest themselves of human affections and loved their own nation, yet that sorrow did not keep them from executing their office boldly; and draws the rule for ministers now, who must follow their course even where the doctrine proves a savour of death.

Quotes an older commentator to the effect that the words are to be said even to those who will not obey, so that they may know what they are and what penalties await them, and observes that faithfulness is cut off out of their mouth rather than out of the heart because their profession of devotion never stopped.

themes: Since the day that your fathers came forth out of the land of Egypt unto this day I have even sent unto you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them:
Yet they hearkened not unto me, nor inclined their ear, but hardened their neck: they did worse than their fathers.
Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee.
But thou shalt say unto them, This is a nation that obeyeth not the voice of the Lord their God, nor receiveth correction: truth is perished, and is cut off from their mouth.

29.pericope_label: Cut off thine hair, O Jerusalem, and cast it away, and take up a lamentation on high places; for the Lord hath rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath. And they have built the high places of Tophet, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I commanded them not. Then will I cause to cease the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness: for the land shall be desolate

schools.summary: Supplies the philology of the shorn hair, the word meaning a crown or diadem and being the one applied to the unshorn locks from which the Nazarite took his name, treats Tophet as no local name at all but a term of contempt substituted for Baal, corrects the English about burial to because there is no room, and reads the closing imagery as characteristic of this prophet, wailing giving way to the utter silence of solitude.

Settles the address from the feminine verb and refuses an emendation that changes the gender through the verse without warrant of manuscript or version, presses the geography of the valley, which lay in the suburbs within sight of the temple so that the guilt was the greater, adds the legal difficulty that a corpse defiled and no sacrifice might be offered near a grave, and defends burial as a custom held sacred in all ages and a symbol of the resurrection.

Reads the command as an order to drop the pretence and throw off the mask, reports and rejects the view that the prophet himself is addressed, derives Tophet from the drum beaten so the parents might not hear the children's cries, and ends on the proportion between such sins and such a punishment.

Turns the figure into a sentence, since Jerusalem had been a Nazarite to God and must now be separated from him as she had been separated to him, and hears defiance in the setting of abominations in the very courts, as though heaven and hell might be reconciled in one place.

debates.question: Who is commanded to cut off the hair?

positions.view: not the prophet but Jerusalem and its inhabitants, since the verb is feminine and the supplement is required
the daughter of Zion, the people addressed as a woman; an emendation changing the gender through the verse is to be refused, having no warrant of manuscript or version
reports the view that the prophet himself is addressed, a Nazarite by his office called to mourn, and rejects it as the less natural construction

debates.question: What is Tophet?

positions.view: named from a drum, beaten so that the parents might not hear the cries of the children
the place in the valley where the continual fires were kept, in and through which they consecrated their children

originally no local name at all but a term of contempt, the word appearing elsewhere for a thing spat upon and substituted for Baal as the shameful thing was elsewhere, since a later repetition of this prediction says the high places of Baal outright
a name that came, with the valley's, to stand for the infernal regions; and the place lay in the suburbs within sight of the temple, so that their guilt was the greater

debates.question: What does the silencing of the marriages signify?

positions.view: a circumlocution for the mirth of the wedding feast, all joy now dumb throughout the land
a part standing for the whole, since without marriages the race cannot continue, so what ceases is all that holds society together
imagery characteristic of this prophet, painting the break-up of a nation's life, wailing giving way to something worse, the utter silence of solitude
a proportion between the sin and the punishment, which must be horrible indeed when it moves God to destroy the work of his own hands

outliers.reading: Turns the Nazarite figure into a sentence on the city, which had been a Nazarite to God and must now be separated from him as she had been separated to him, for it is time that those who have lost their holiness should lay aside their joy; and hears defiance in the setting of abominations in the very courts, as though heaven and hell might be reconciled in one place.

Corrects the clause about burial to because there is no room, and observes that the dead will be laid precisely where both parties would have avoided burying, the ground being sacred to the worshippers of Molech and accursed to the worshippers of the Lord; and traces the history of the abominations in the house from Ahaz through Manasseh to a probable relapse when Josiah's death left the idolatrous party free.

themes: Cut off thine hair, O Jerusalem, and cast it away, and take up a lamentation on high places; for the Lord hath rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.
For the children of Judah have done evil in my sight, saith the Lord: they have set their abominations in the house which is called by my name, to pollute it.

And they have built the high places of Tophet, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart.

Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that it shall no more be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter: for they shall bury in Tophet, till there be no place.
And the carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth; and none shall fray them away.

Then will I cause to cease from the cities of Judah, and from the streets of Jerusalem, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride: for the land shall be desolate.
